title: Amundsen and Scott Race to the Pole
text:
In 1910 two expeditions set out for the South Pole. The British party was led by Robert Falcon Scott. The Norwegian Roald Amundsen had announced he was going to the Arctic, then, after news that Americans had reached the North Pole, he secretly turned south and informed Scott by telegram that he was heading for Antarctica.

The two men prepared differently. Amundsen had spent years in the Arctic, including two winters with the Netsilik Inuit, from whom he learned to use dogs, to dress in loose fur clothing and to travel efficiently. He took expert skiers and dog drivers and nearly a hundred dogs, planning to kill some along the way to feed the others and the men. He laid depots of food and marked them with lines of flags across his route so they could be found in poor visibility.

Scott relied on a mix of motor sledges, Siberian ponies, some dogs and, in the end, men pulling sledges themselves. The motor sledges broke down and the ponies suffered in the cold and had to be shot.

Amundsen's party of five reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911 and returned safely. Scott's party of five reached it on 17 January 1912 and found the Norwegian tent. On the long march back, slowed by illness, injury, short rations and severe cold, all five died. Scott's last diary entries were found with his body months later.
lesson: Preparation that borrows the best knowledge of those who know the terrain beats courage and effort alone. Choose methods proven in the conditions you will face.
source: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole (1912); Scott's Last Expedition: The Journals (1913); Roland Huntford, Scott and Amundsen (1979)
caveat: Historians still debate how much of Scott's failure was due to his choices and how much to unusually severe weather on the return march.
